newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Anti-Taleban alliance on ropes, but could survive.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Taleban alliance on ropes, but could survive.

text.p: A northern alliance fighting Afghanistan's rampant Islamic Taleban militia is showing serious signs of collapse, but it is too soon to write off its chances of survival, analysts said on Sunday.

The Taleban, who have taken over two-thirds of war-ravaged Afghanistan in the two years since the movement was born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan, have thundered forward in major military advances over the last 10 days.
Ahmad Shah Masood, defence chief in the government ousted from Kabul by the Taleban in September, is penned up again in his Panjsher Valley stronghold north of the capital.

His ally, one-time foe Abdul Rashid Dostum, is watching black-turbanned Taleban fighters thrust up the Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush mountains which guard his northern domain as raging inflation threatens dissatisfaction from within.

"The Taleban have made it clear they're not interested in peace talks and that they plan to go on to military victory, but whether they can do that is very unclear," said one military analyst who asked not to be identified.

"Anyone who's brave enough to forecast what's going to happen in Afghanistan is a seriously deluded person," said another, reflecting on 18 years of war in Afghanistan which have taken numerous bewildering twists.

The analysts said the Taleban advance had involved little hand-to-hand fighting and it was possible Masood had gone back to the Panjsher, to which he retreated after the fall of Kabul, because his men were too exposed where they were.

Unable to move forward with Dostum's ethnic Uzbek forces not fully committed to the battle, Masood's ethnic Tajiks were strung out across a flat valley floor with a deadly cold winter tightening its grip, they said.
"From the Panjsher, he can do what he does best, guerrilla warfare," said one analyst. "The Soviet army couldn't get him out of there (in the 1980s) and I doubt the Taleban can."
The military analyst said the Taleban would have great difficulty taking the six northern provinces Dostum holds.

"Dostum is the one Afghan commander conventionally organised and armed and the flat terrain north of the Hindu Kush gives the advantage to conventional warfare, plus his men will be fighting for their homes," he said.

Nevertheless, the largely ethnic Pushtun Taleban have succeeded in capturing much of Afghanistan without major fighting in a campaign committed to bringing their stern version of Islam's Sharia law to the whole country.
"They've done it by subversion and buying commanders with a combination of money and threats. It's possible they could do it to Dostum with all the problems he's facing now," said another analyst.
Jean-Luc Paludini of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) told reporters in Kabul last week that month-on-month inflation had soared to 140 percent in Mazar-i-Sharif, Dostum's capital.
"It must be terrible to live in Mazar," he said. Another Western aid official said many people had not been paid for months.

The analysts said Dostum's commanders were selling the currency printed by their leader -- and not valid in Taleban-held areas -- for dollars in what could be interpreted as signs of getting ready to flee.
But one said Taleban agents could be buying up dollars -- a currency widely held in Afghanistan's major cities as a safety net -- to undermine morale.
"They've done this very successfully before and if people can't get dollars it undermines confidence in the economy and, inevitably, the leadership," he said.
